In accordance with WAC 456- 10- 730, APpellant has filed an
exception to the Proposed Decision issued on May 13, 1996,
following a hearing conducted on APril 23, 1996, by Gerrald
Dillard, Presiding Officer, Board of Tax APpeals ( Board)
In order for this Board to reconsider the findings set forth
in the Proposed Decision, it must be clear that the Proposed
Decision did not properly consider the evidence or that there was
an omission of certain pertinent facts.
The Board reviewed the written exceptions, the Proposed
Decision issued concerning this appeal, and all available informa-
tion and data We conclude that the issues raised by Appellant
were adequately met in the Proposed Decision and that the evidence
was properly considered. This Board finds no basis for changing
the decision. Therefore, we deny the exceptions and adopt the
Proposed Decision as the Final De,~ s:~~ o~ this Board.

Board now makes its decision as follows:

ISSUE
The issue in this appeal is the January I, 1995, true and fair
market value ot a parcel of land located at 1201 Ocean Shores Blvd.
S. W. ( Division 18, Lot 1, Block 1). There is a one- story
improvement with garage and basement located on this parcel of
land. The Board of Equalization determined the land value to be
87, 000 and the improvement value $ 119, 770 for a total value of
206, 770. The Owner' s opinion of value is land, $ 75, 000;
improvement. $ 92, 200; for a total property value of $186, 104. The
Owner contends that the total property value, in his opinion, is
175, 000.

FAr~~ AND CONTRNTIONS
In determining the value of this appeal, the Owner has relied
on relating to assessed values of other properties as compared to
the assessed value of the subject. The Owner introduced one sale
indicating a sale price of $ 145, 000 and noted that the assessment
on this property is $158, 610. He stated this property is located
1, 140 feet from the subject property. The Owner argued the
comparable sales used by the Assessor are not reliable indicators
of value because of many varying reasons. He stated that sales
activity within the area of the subject is stagnant. He agreed
that many properties in the area are better than the subject but
noted, from his observation, they are assessed similar to the
subject. He argued the Assessor used multi- family properties as
comparable sales to the subject. The Owner said the subject
improvement was self constructed some 17 years ago. He said the
roof of the improvement needs some repair and other repairs are
needed. He also stated the current assessment of $58. 99 per square
foot, as determined by the Assessor, is high when compared to other
assessments in the area.
In support of his arguments relating to the assessed values,
the Owner provided the following:
Washington Constitution Art 7, Sec. 1 ( amendment 14)
All taxes shall be uniform upon the same class of
property within the territorial limits of the authority
levying the tax .
Washington State Supreme Court Statement: " It seems too
plain for argument that to pick out the property of a
particular owner and raise the assessed valuation of his
property substantially above the assessed valuation of
property similarly situated, violates the uniformity and
equality provision of article VII, Sec. 2, of the state
constitution. . . . If the assessment is higher than that
of property of like character and similar in situation,
the assessment cannot be sustained, even though it be
based on the true market value of the property. II Pier
Q.1. L . _.. Inc: v 5i.n? r:~_'}~~89~~Wn,. 2d 379, 373 P. 2d 2 ( 1977).
Citations omitted.)
The Assessor valued the subject of this appeal based upon the
market data approach. He said he looked through sales which he
considered to be mo~t appropriate in valuing the subject of this
appeal as of the assessment date. The Assessor introduced three
sales along with all the data relating to each of the sales for
this Board' s consideration. He provided photographs so this Board
could determine the comparison between those properties which had
sold as compared to the subject property.

Additionally, the Assessor provided bare land sales for this
Board' s consideration in determining the true and fair land value.
Additional comments offered by the Assessor are:
Mr. Jackson mentioned on his petition that his
neighbor' s land was assessed at a lower value than his.
This is correct. The reason for the difference in value
is that his neighbor' s parcel is located in Division 17A
while Mr. Jackson' s home is located in Division 18. When
reviewing the ocean front sales, it is very apparent that
as you move south up the beach toward the jetty, the
values per front foot of ocean increase. Because of
this, the values placed on the ocean front lots are
staggered upward as you move south toward the jetty. One
of the dividing lines was set between Div 17A and Div 18,
because at the time the land values were set, neither
Division 17 or 17A had land sales as high as Division 18.
However, one land sale did occur in Div 17A for $87, 000
in the early part of May 1995."
ANALYSTS AND ~ OrN.[U"SIONS
This BoardIs goal in its hearings is the acquisition of
sufficient, accurate evidence to support a determination of true
and fair value as defined by statute ( RCW 84. 40. 030) and the
Washington Administrative Code ( WAC 458- 12- 301) .
The owner contends that inequities exist with respect to the
assessed value of the property when compared with assessed values
of similar properties in the area. Exact equality is neither
possible nor required. Satnr v. Oenartment of Revenu~, 89 Wn. 2d
338, 572 P. 2d 1094 ( 1977).
Evidence presented at the hearing does not show that the
Assessor has overvalued the Owner' s property. This Board does not
have statutory power of equalization. This Board' s jurisdiction is
restricted to reviewing the action of the County Board of
Equalization for the specific property under appeal and determining
its true and fair value in accordance with the guidelines of RCW
84. 40. 030.
While we understand the Owner' s concerns regarding
equalization, this Board has no jurisdiction in such matters. We
are restricted by law to reviewing the action of the County Board
of Equalization for the specific property under appeal and
determining its market value in accordance with RCW 84. 40. 030. The
Owner1s comparison of sale prices and assessed valuations does not
offer any insights into the specific market value of the subject
propert.y.
PROPOSED DECISION - Page 3 Docket No. 48312

RCW 84. 40. 030 states that property must be valued at 100
percent of its true and fair value based upon sales of the subject
property or similar properties made within the past five years.
The appraisal shall consider the extent to which the sale of a
similar property actually represents the general effective market
demand for property of such type in the geographical area in which
such property is located. The appraisal shall also be consistent
with land use plans, zoning, and ap-y other governmental policies or
practices in effect at the time of appraisal that affect the use of
property, as well as physical and environmental influences.
True and fair value is " market value", that is, the price
to be paid by a willing buyer to a willing seller. Carkonen v.
Williams, 76 Wn. 2d 617, 458 P. 2d 280 ( 1969).
This Board has carefully reviewed the market data entered by
each party with significant notice given to the sales data provided
by the Assessor. The sales provided by the Assessor are briefly
outlined as follows:

1994 and reflected site values ranging from $ 85, 000 to $97, 400.
Recognizing that this BoardIs jurisdiction is to determine
true and tair market value as of the assessment date at issue, it
is this Boardt s conclusion that the evidence provided by the
Assessor does support the value of land and improvements
established by the action of the Grays Harbor County Board of
Equalization.
This Board wishes to add that we recognize the confusion of
the Owner, when looking to assessed value as being relevant
evidence. However, we must emphasize that this is beyond the
Board' s Jurisdiction for consideration.
PROPOSED DECISION - Page 4 Docket No. 48312

DECISION
The decision of the Grays Harbor County Board of Equalization
is affirmed. This Board finds that the true and fair value of the
subject property is $206, 770.
The Grays Harbor County Assessor and Treasurer are hereby
directed that the assessment and tax rolls of Grays Harbor County
are to accord with and give full effect to the provisions of this
decision.

Dear Mr. Smith:
Receipt of your appeal from action by the King County Board of
Equalization is acknowledged. We regret that your appeal cannot be
set for hearing.
This Board must adhere strictly to the limitations provided in
RCW 84. 08. 130( 1). This section of the law permits any property
owner to appeal an action of any county board of equalization " by
filing with the board of tax appeals a notice of appeal within
thirty days after the mailing of the decision of such board of
equalization."
The determination of value relating to your appeal was mailed
by the county board of equalization on August 29, 1995. Your
notice of appeal, filed with this office, was postmarked on
September 29, 1995. Since the information in the file shows that
your appeal was not filed within the 3D- day time period. it cannot
be heard by this Board. Jurisdiction of the Board is limited by
statute and any action by this Board outside this area of
jurisdiction would be declared invalid.
However, if you believe that the Board does have jurisdiction
to hear this matter, you may file an exception that must be
received by the Board within 20 days from the date of this letter.
If no exception is filed, then this decision will be final.

This matter came before William Terhaar, presiding for the
Board of Tax Appeals ( Board), for an informal hearing on
August 21, 1996. Appellant, Rolf Borgerson ( Owner), was not
present but was represented by David Ebenger, Attorney, via
telephone conference call. James White appeared for Respondent,
James Hand, Okanogan County Assessor ( Assessor).
This Board heard the testimony, reviewed the evidence, and
considered the arguments made on behalf of both parties. This
Board now makes its decision as follows:

The issue in this appeal is the January 1, 1994, true and fair
value of the 10. 61 acres of undeveloped land located on East County
Road in Winthrop, Washington.
FACTS ANn CONTF.NTTONS
The subject property is a 10. 61 acre parcel located south of
Winthrop on the East County Road. The parcel is served with
irrigation water and has good access to t.he site. Electrical
service is readily available. The site has not been perc tested
and there is no well or domestic water system.

The Assessor originally valued the subject property at $61, 800
for the 1994, 1995, 1996 and 1997 revaluation cycle. This value
was upheld by the Okanogan County Board of Equalization. The Owner
appealed to this Board contending a value of $42, 000.
In support of a reduced valuation, the Owner is appealing to
this Board for two reasons. First, the Assessor' s comparable sales
are of five-acre parcels and are not comparable. Second, the
Assessor' s comparable sales are all located within a completed
short plat. Short-platted land is not comparable because of the
value- added features that short plats enjoy. Those features
include access and internal roads, domestic water, surveyed
parcels, pere tests, electrical service, and guaranteed use as a
single- family site. The Owner stated that this takes from twelve
to eighteen months to complete. The SUbject property does not have
any of these value- added features. The OWner presented five
comparable sales from the same area that transpired between
September 1989 and October 1993. The sales are of flat
agricultural land within one mile of the subject. The range in
value is $2, 799 to $4, 000 per acre. The parcels range in size from
10. 5 acres to 14. 29 acres.
In support of the Assessor' s valuation, the Assessor presented
four comparable sales from a short plat that is adjacent to the
subject property. The Assessor stated that these sales were used
because of their close proximity to the subject. Also, this short
plat was platted in 1991, which was prior to the current
regulations that became effective in 1992. The current regulations
require a domestic water system for each lot within the short plat.
The comparable sales selected by the Assessor are not improved with
domestic water.
The four comparable sales have a range in value of $33, 000 to
50, 000. The parcels range in size from 5. 04 acres to 5. 62 acres.
The sales transpired between September 1991 and March 1994. These
sales indicate an average price per acre of $ 7, 750. The Assessor
stated that the short-platted land is assessed at $ 6, 500 per acre
and the subject property is assessed at $ 5, 825 per acre.
In rebuttal the Assessor stated that the Owner' s comparable
sales were not received in a timely manner. They were received by
the Okanogan County Asse~.sor on August 19, 1996 .
There was considerable discussion between the Owner and the
Assessor as to which of the Owner' s comparable sales are relevant
in this appeal. The sales that the Owner submitted to the Okanogan
County Board of Equalization were discussed. The Assessor stated
that of the ten comparable sales submitted, three were presented at
this hearing. One comparable has the wrong parcel number and
cannot be identified. A second sale is entirely within the flood
plain. A third sale is up Benson Creek. A fourth comparable is on
PROPOSED DECISION - Page 2 Docket No. 48315

the other side of the river in a totally different neighborhood.
A fifth sale is of a I3- acre parcel of which only 4 acres is usable
and there is no access. The Assessor stated that there is only one
good comparable out of the ten. It was a 1989 sale of 10. 5 acres
for $39, 500. However, the sale was not submitted in time to be
used in this appeal.
The Owner stated that the four comparable sales submitted by
the Assessor should not be considered as they are too small. There
are two wells serving the short-platted land that the Assessor used
as a comparable sale. In closing, the Owner contended that $3, 555
per acre is the appropriate value per acre based on his comparable
sales.
The Assessor clarified that there was no rounding or averaging
of values. The mass appraisal system requires the development of
a land schedule to be used on different types of land. The various
portions of the subject property were valued accordingly. All of
the components do in fact, average out to $5, 825 per acre.
AINSALYAN.';D CONCLUSIONS
This Board, giving full opportunity for all arguments and
having considered all testimony and documentary evidence submitted
by the parties in support of their respective positions, hereby
enters the following analysis and conclusions:
The assessor is required to establish the true and fair value
of residential property based upon sales of the subject property or
sales of comparable properties made within the past five years.
RCW 84. 40. 030. True and fair value is " market value", that is, the
price to be paid by a willing buyer to a willing seller. rarkonen
v. Wi.lliams, 76 Wn. 2d 617, 458 P. 2d 280 ( 1969).
Under RCW 84. 40. 0301, the valuation placed on property by the
assessor is presumed to be correct, and can only be overcome upon
presentation by the taxpayer of clear, cogent, and convincing
evidence that the assessor' s valuation of the subject property is
erroneous. " Clear, cogent, and convincing" evidence means a
quantum of proof which is less than beyond a reasonable doubt, but
more than a mere preponderance of the evidence. It is the quantum
of evidence necessary to convince the trier of fact that the
ultimate fact in issue is " highly probable". Tn re Sean, 82 Wn. 2d
736, 513 P. 2d 831 ( 1973).
In our review of the evidence and the testimony submitted, we
have considered all of the comparable sales presented. Consistent
with our policy of review, this Board has given most weight to
chose sales located nearest the subject, judged to be most similar,
and which occurred closest to the valuation date at issue.
PROPOSED DECISION - Page 3 Docket No. 48315

pF.CISION
This Board finds that the Owner has not presented the clear,
cogent, and convincing evidence necessary to overcome the
presumptive correctness of the value established by the Assessor.
We, therefore, sustain the value established by the Assessor. This
Board orders the value of the subject property to be as set forth
on page one of this decision; provided, that the Assessor may
revalue the subject property for 1995, 1996, and 1997 under the
provisions of RCW 36. 21. 080 ( new construction)
The Okanogan County Assessor is hereby directed that the
assessment and tax rolls of Okanogan County are to accord with and
give full effect to the provisions of this decision.

This matter came before Edward McKenna, presiding for the
Board of Tax Appeals ( Board), for an informal hearing on April 15.
1996. Appellants, Martin and Elaine Standel ( Owners), were
represented by Martin Standel. Wendy Morse appeared for
Respondent, Scott Noble, King County Assessor ( Assessor). Traci K.
Williams, King County Assessor' s Office, was an observer.
This Board heard the testimony, reviewed the evidence, and
considered the arguments made on behalf of both parties. This
Board now makes its decision as follows:

The issue in this appeal is the true and fair value of the
subject property on the date of assessment, January 1, 1994.
FACTS AND CONTENTIONS
The subject of this appeal is all, 548 square foot parcel,
zoned R3. 5, located in the Forest Ridge Development in King County.
The subject is improved with a four-bedroom, two- story, 100 percent
frame home built in 1989. The home contains 3, 150 square feet of
finished living area and is judged to be Grade 10 construction
quality in average condition.
This hearing follows the action of the King County Board of
Equalization which sustained the total value as determined by the

Assessor. The Owners appealed that decision to this Board
contending the total value to be 260, 000 land $ 60, 000,
improvements $ 200, 000).
The Owners contend that the Assessor has failed to adequately
consider the reduction in the size of the back yard of the subject
due to the county taking a lS- foot strip of land for the use of a
jogging trail. The OWners argue that the reduction in size of the
back yard significantly reduces the overall value of the subject
due to its unusual size and shape as a " flag lot". In support of
their contention of value the Owners rely upon a news article
appearing in the Seattle Times dated February 1994. The article
indicates that Puget Sound home prices increased an average of only
1. 6 percent for the year 1993. The Owners further rely upon the
sale of the neighboring property that sold three times within the
past several years at a sale price of $255, 000. The Owners contend
that the grade difference between this sale and the subject is
negligible, and the most recent sale of this neighboring parcel was
during a " relevant time" of this appeal. No further information
was provided regarding this sale.
The Assessor presented a chart showing sixteen sales of
similar properties occurring close to the lien date. The Assessor
argues that all are similar on the exterior with some interior
differences accounting for minor grade variations. These sales
within the subject plat range from $245, 000 to $315, 000. Each lot
is considered a building site and, the Assessor argues, the market
does not recognize a difference for " flagll lots. Of those sixteen
sales, the Assessor relies upon three as being the most comparable
to the subject. Sale No. 1 is a 17, 130 square foot parcel located
one block south of subject. This parcel is improved with a 3, 040
square foot, two- bedroom home built in 1989 and sold in August 1993
for $282, 500. Sale No. 2 is a 12, 255 square foot parcel located
one block west of the subject. This parcel is improved with a
2, 800 square foot, two~bedroom home built in 1989 and sold in
August 1993 for $270, 000. Sale NO. 3 is a 16, 379 square foot
parcel located one block east of the subject. This parcel is
improved with a 2, 870 square foot, two- bedroom home built in 1989
and sold in March 1994 for $278, 800. The Assessor notes that Sale
No. 1 is flag lot similar to the subject while Sale No. 3 also had
a portion of its lot taken for the jogging track. The Assessor
contends that each of these sales is similar in style, room count,
and quality of construction. The Assessor argues that the OWner' s
sale is too distant to be considered a reliable indicator of value.
ANALYSIS AND CONCJ.nSTONS
This Board, giving full opportunity for all arguments and
having considered all testimony and documentary evidence submitted
by the parties in support of their respective positions, hereby
enters the following analysis and conclusions:
PROPOSED DECISION - Page 2 Docket No. 48316

The Assessor is required to establish the true and fair value
of residential property based upon sales of the subject property or
sales of comparable properties made within the past five years.
RCW 84. 40. 030. True and fair value is "market value", that is, the
price to be paid by a willing buyer to a willing seller. Carkon~n
v_ Williams, 76 Wn. 2d 617, 458 P. 2d 280 ( 1969).
Under RCW 84. 40. 0301, the valuation placed on property by the
Assessor is presumed to be correct, and can only be overcome upon
presentation by the taxpayer of clear, cogent, and convincing
evidence that the assessor' s valuation of the subject property is
erroneous. IIClear, cogent and convincing" evidence means a quantum
of proof which is less than beyond a reasonable doubt, but more
than a mere preponderance of the evidence. It is the quantum of
evidence necessary to convince the trier of fact that the ultimate
fact in issue is " highly probable". In re g~aq, 82 Wn. 2d 736, 513
P. 2d 831 ( 1973).
The sales comparison approach is based on the premise that
the market value of a property is directly related to the prices of
comparable, competitive properties. The value of a property in the
market is set by the availability of substitute properties of
similar utility and desirability." Appraisal Institute, . IM.
AnnraiAal of Rp.~l ERtatp. 403 ( 10th ed. 1992)
In our review of the comparable sales provided, this Board
gives the most weight to those sales located nearest to the
subject, judged to be most similar, occurring closest to the
January 1, 1994 valuation date in question. After reviewing those
sales presented, we find those sales presented by the Assessor to
be similar in location, and comparable in age, style and quality of
construction. Considering the range in value from $ 270, 000 to
282, 500, we find the total value of the subject as determined by
the Assessor to be well supported.
Although the arguments made on behalf of the Owners are
interesting and persuasive, they lack documentation. RCW
84. 40. 0301 (1) clearly states that the burden is on those who
challenge the Assessor' s valuation. Although the Owners provided
some information regarding comparable sales, this Board requires
specific information regarding those sales and their comparability
to the subject. Without specific market evidence, this Board has
no alternative other than to find that the Owner has not presented
the clear, cogent and convincing evidence necessary to overcome the
presumption of correctness of the value established by the
Assessor.

Owners' absence was not prejudicial to their case. The written

ANAT,VSTS AND CONCLTTSTONS
This BoardIs goal in its hearings is the acquisition of
sufficient, accurate evidence to support a determination of true
and fair value as defined by statute ( RCW 84. 40. 030) and the
Washington Administrative Code ( WAC 458- 12- 301).
The valuation placed on the property by the assessor is
presumed to be correct, and can only be overcome by presentation of
clear, cogent, and convincing evidence that the value is erroneous.
RCW 84. 40. 0301; Weverhaeuspr roo v. Eastp~, 126 Wn. 2d 370, 894 P. 2d
1290 ( 1995). " Clear, cogent, and convincing" evidence means a
quantum of proof which is less than beyond a reasonable doubt, but
more than a mere preponderance of the evidence. It is the quantum
of evidence necessary to convince the trier of fact that the
ultimate fact in issue is " highly probable". In re SeaD, 82 Wn. 2d
736, 513 P. 2d 831 ( 1973).
When available, comparable sales are the preferred evidence of
value. Comparable sales closest to the lien date are given the
most weight.
Market value is best derived from the analysis of sales of
similar properties. Income and cost approaches will only be given
substantial weight in the absence of adequate market data.
This Board has carefully reviewed the arguments set forth in
the Owners' petition and has considered the evidence entered into
the record by the Assessor. For ad valorem tax purposes real
property must be assessed at 100 percent of its indicated true and
fair value. We find that, from the analysis of the sales
introduced by the Assessor, the current assessment of the subject
property does not exceed its true and fair value.

This Board finds that the Owners have not presented the clear,
cogent, and convincing evidence necessary to overcome the
presumptive correctness of the value established by the Assessor.
We, therefore, sustain the value established by the Assessor.

ISSUES
The issues in these appeals are the true and fair values of
land and improvements identified as Parcel No. 272601- 1- 008- 2004.
The property is described as a single- family residence, one and
one- half 3tory, with a full basement and an attached double garage.
The residence is situated on a parcel of land containing . 81 acre.
Additional improvements are a boathouse, piling, float and ramp,
and a concrete bulkhead of 300 lineal feet.

FACT~ AND CONTENTIONS
The Owner' s arguments, set forth in Exhibit A- I, primarily
relate to his contended inability to meet the increases in property
tax assessments. This, he stated, is because he is retired and on
a fixed income.
The Owner stated that in searching for sales of similar
properties at the Assessor' s office. he was u.nable to find any
sales which he believes to be comparable to the subject. A further
search for comparable sales made through a private appraiser' s
office failed to disclose any comparable sales. The subject:.
residence was originally built in ~9S4 and remodeled in 1980. The
Assessor' s 25 percent depreciation factor is, in his opinion,
inadequate for a home which is 43 years old. He contended that the
comparable sales used by the Assessor are not similar to the
subject and do not serve to fairly indicate the value of the
subject property. Further, conditions which he contends would
affect the value are its location on Liberty Bay which, he says, is
one of the most polluted bodies of water in the Puget Sound area.
The Assessor testified that the value of the subject property
had been determined by the market data approach. The Assessor
stated that her office is very concerned about the increasing
values and makes extensive efforts to value all properties
according to the value as indicated in the marketplace and as
required by Washington statutes.
The Assessor stated the valuation of this property changed in
1994 for taxes payable in 1995 under the Kitsap County Assessor' s
Cyclical Revalll-3tion Program. The Assessor said, at the Owner' s
request, a reexamination was made of the property on October 13,
1993, with the Owner present and a complete verification of all
property characteristics was made.
To support the current assessed value, the Assessor introduced
three sales for this Board' s consideration. These sales, in their
brief form, are as follows:
Sale No. 1 is a property located near the subject and
similar in most respects. This sale indicated a value of
235, 000 and was consummated in Februa;~ 1994. The land
is . 50 acre with 50 waterfront feet. The improvement was
constructed in 1922 and is a one and one- half story
design.
Sale No. 2 is a single- family residence which sold for
254, 000 in April 1994. This site is . 38 acre with 8Q
waterfront feet. It is considered to be similar to the

subject. The improvement was constructed in 1974 and is
of multi-story design.
Sale NO. 3 is of a property which sold for $160, 000 in
December 1994. The land is described as . 47 acre with 75
waterfront feet. The improvement is a single- family
residence which was constructed in 1970. It is a
Rambler" design.
The Assessor stated that, when considering these three sales,
adjustments were made for date of sale, location, utility of site,
age of improvement, and other factors normally considered in the
appraisal process.
The Assessor also said that these three sales were chosen
because of their close proximity to the subject and the dates of
sale. The Assessor noted that her Sale No. 2 was given most weight
in the valuation process.
ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS
The Assessor is required to establish the true and fair value
of property based upon sales of the subject property or sales of
comparable properties made within the past five years. RCW
84. 40. 030. True and fair value is " market value". that is. the
price to be paid by a willing buyer to a willing seller. Carkonen
v. William~, 76 Wn. 2d 617, 458 P. 2d 280 ( 1969).
Accrued depreciation is the difference between the
reproduction or replacement cost of the improvements on the
effective date of the appraisal and the market value of the
improvements on the same date. Depreciation is caused by
deterioration or obsolescence in the property. Deterioration is
evidenced by wear and tear on the structure. Functional
obsolescence is caused by internal property characteristics such as
a poor floor plan, inadequate mechanical equipment, or functional
inadequacy or superadequacy due to size or other characteristics.
External obsolescence is caused by conditions outside the property
such as a lack of demand. Changing property uses in the area, or
national economic conditions. Some types of depreciation interact
with one another and the analysis of depreciation from all causes
is cumulative. Appraisal Institute. Thp Annrai~al of Real F.~tate
320 ( 10th ed. 1992).
The value of property for purposes of ad valorem taxation is
Umarket value", that is: " the amount of money which a purchaser
willing, but not obligated, to buy would pay an owner willing, but
not obligated, to sell, taking into consideration all uses to which
the property is adapted and might in reason be applied." Mason

County Overtaxed. Inc. v. Mason Countv, 62 Wn. 2d 677, 683- 84, 384
P. 2d 352 ( 1963); accord, Carknn~n v. Williams, 76 Wn. 2d 617, 458
P. 2d 280 ( 1969).
In the evaluation of the evidence, as presented by the Owner,
this Board finds no conclusive evidence which would relate
specifically to the true and fair value of the subject of this
appeal.
The Assessor has met the mandate of the Washington statutes by
relating sales of similar properties and adjusting those sales to
best reflect the value of the subject property as of the assessment
date. The Assessor provided adequate data relating to each of the
sales which she considered so that this Board may make a complete
review of the sales and determine the reliability of the evidence.
We find the evidence presented by the Assessor to
substantially support the values of both land and improvements as
set forth in the Kitsap County Board of Equalization orders for
each assessment year.
pECISTON
In Docket Nos. 48324 and 49061, the Owner' s petition is
denied. The values for land and improvements, as determined by the
Kitsap County Board of Equalization, are affirmed.
The Kitsap County Assessor and Treasurer are hereby directed
that the assessment and tax rolls of Kitsap County are to accord
with and give full effect to the provisions of this decision.

Bank ( Seafirstl. Michael D. Jolly, Deputy Assessor, appeared for

ISSUE
The issue in this appeal is the January 1, 1994, true and fair
value of the Seafirst bank property located at 301 NE Northgate
Way, Seattle, Washington. The Assessor valued the subject property
at $ 1, 743, 300, which was sustained by the Board of Equalization.
Seafirst appealed to this Board contending a value of $1, 345, 000.
FACTS AND CONTENTIONS
The subject property is located within the Northgate Mall, at
the far north end. The property consists of a separate pad type
parcel, 9, 367 square feet in size. The parcel has a " NC385/1'
commercial zoning classification. Improvements consist of a one-
story, masonry, branch bank building, built in 1951. The building,
which includes a 8, 906 square foot unfinished basement, has a first
floor rentable area of 8, 956 square feet. The Assessor lists the

building as good in construction quality and states the bank is a
modern looking facility due to various renovations.
Seafirst explained that although the subject is located within
the Northgate Malll a long corridor separates the bank from the
main mall. Also, this branch bank has no drive-up banking
facilities, and drive-up banking is not possible at this location.
To support its contended value, Seafirst relied on the sales
comparison approach. Seafirst provided ten branch bank sales.
Seafirst reviewed these sales, noting Sales Nos. 1 and 7 are given
little weight due to the less than arm' B length nature of the
transactions, Sale No. 2 has excess land, and Sale No. 3 has a
corner pad Southcenter Mall location. These ten properties sold
between September 1992 and March 1995, reflecting price per square
foot of building area indications ranging from $103. 44 to $189. 05.
Based on these sales, Seafirst concludes a value of $150 per square
foot is indicated for the subject, resulting in a value of
1, 345, 000.
Seafirst also provided data on eight recently negotiated
branch bank leases. These leases reflect annual lease rates
ranging from $ 10 to $ 20. 42 per square foot. Seafirst did not
include an income analysis of the subject, stating these leases
were provided as back-up information.
The Assessor explained he valued the subject as a portion of
the Northgate Mall economic unit. He described the subject as
having a good location at the north end of the mall and that the
subject could easily be remodeled into retail space.
The Assessor provided his original appraisal of the entire
mall, which includes three spreadsheets showing the various
portions of the mall and their values. He stated the cost and
income approaches were used, with most weight given to the income
approach. The Assessor stated the subject' s assessed value was
based on an economic lease rate of $24. 00 per square foot and an
8. 75 percent overall capitalization rate. To support his economic
lease rate, the AsseSBor cited a $ 22 per square foot branch bank
lease ( which he adjusted upward for the subject' s mall location)
and stated the going retail lease rate range in the mall is $22 to
24 per square foot.
The Assessor also included three comparable sales. These
sales reflect price per square foot of rentable area indications
ranging from $173. 41 to $235. 02. The Assessor believes these sales
have inferior locations, and noted it is difficult to find "clean"
bank sales due to the numerous bank mergers and resulting swapping
of assets. The Assessor concludes both the income and market
approaches support his assessed value at $194. 65 per square foot of
building area.
PROPOSED DECISION - Page 2 Docket No. 48325

In response to Seafirst' s arguments and evidence, the Assessor
stated: 1) if the subject was a detached bank branch, he would not
have used an 8. 75 percent overall rate; and 2) because it is
connected to the mall, the Assessor contends it is appropriate to
value the subject as part of the mall.
In rebuttal, Seafirst stated: 1) it was unable to reach the
subject' s specific assessed value from the Assessor' s total mall
analysis; 2) Seafirst contends the lease rate for its Lake Forest
Park branch is $15 per square foot, not the $ 22 per square foot
amount cited by the Assessor; 3) compared to the other branch bank
comparables, the subject has no drive-up banking facilities and
Seafirst developed a separate drive-up facility across the street,
valued at $600, 000; and 4) the subject is not retail space now and
conversion would require renovation costs.
ANALYSTS AND CONCT,tJSIONS
This Board, giving full opportunity for all arguments and
having considered all testimony and documentary evidence submitted
by the parties in support of their respective positions, hereby
enters the following analysis and conclusions:
Under the provisions of RCW 84. 40. 030 and WAC 458- 12- 301, the
true and fair value of property shall be based upon sales of the
subject property or sales of comparable properties made within the
past five years. In addition, consideration may be given to cost,
cost less depreciation, and the capitalization of income that would
be derived from prudent use of the property. True and fair value
is "market value," that is, the price to be paid by a willing buyer
to a willing seller. ~ arkonen v. William~, 76 Wn. 2d 617, 458 P. 2d
280 ( 1969).
The valuation placed on the property by the Assessor is
presumed to be correct, and can only be overcome by presentation of
clear, cogent and convincing evidence that the value is erroneous.
RCW 84. 40. 0301( 1).
The Assessor primarily relied on an income analysis of the
entire mall to support his contended value for the subject. This
Board understands the mass appraisal nature of the Assessor' s work
and the reasons for including the subject within this overall mall
analysis. However, like Seafirst, we t.oo had a difficult time
equating this overall analysis to a specific value for the subject.
Another problem is the issue of land value contributions within
this overall mall analysis, especially considering the subject' s
small ( pad) land size. This issue was not addressed. Also,
although the Assessor discussed economic lease rates in general, no
specific data regarding these properties was provided ( such as
size, location, etc.) to enable effective consideration. Seafirst
PROPOSED DECISION - Page 3 Docket No. 48325

did not provide an income analysis, but did submit actual branch
bank lease data for consideration.
After review of the information provided, we believe the sales
submitted by the parties provide the best market evidence. Of the
sales provided, most weight is given to Assessor' s Sale No. 3 and
Seafirst' s Sales Nos. 3 and 4. Two of these sales are located
close to the subject on NE Northgate Way, and the other is adjacent
to Southcenter Mall. These sales reflect price per square foot of
rentable area indications of $173, $ 158 and $ 146. While we agree
with the Assessor' s position that the subject' s location within the
mall is a plus, the subject' s lack of drive-up banking facilities
should also be considered. Overall, we conclude the market
evidence supports a value of $1, 522, 500 for the subject -- $ 170. 00
per square foot.
DECISION
The decision of the Board of Equalization is set aside. Based
on the evidence provided, this Board finds that the true and fair
value of the Subject property, as of January 1, 1994, is
1, 522, 500, as set forth on page one of this decision.
The King County Assessor is hereby directed that the
assessment and tax rolls of King County are to accord with and give
full effect to the provisions of this decision.

ISSUES
In Docket No. 48326, the issue involves only the land value,
which is an adjoining parcel to the primary subject of these
appeals. The parties agreed, by stipulating, that the value of the
land parcel is $ 42, 350. No specific testimony was offered in
support. Therefore, this Board accepts that value and orders the
appropriate assessment rolls to reflect accordingly.
The remainder of this decision will relate to the issue set
forth in Docket No. 48327, described as Parcel No. 112401- 3- 074-
2009. The issue involved is the true and fair market value of a
73- unit apartment building known as the Colonial Manor. The Board

of Equalization determined a land value of $ 420, 000 and an
improvement value of $ 1, 243, 000. It is GDR' s position that the
value is $ 1, 300, 000 which it states is for both parcels. This
Board takes this to mean also the parcel described in Docket No.
48326.
FA= S AND CONTENTIONS
It was essentially agreed by each party that the subject
property has poor access, suffers a high vacancy rate, and has a
high turn around of tenants. Most of the units are furnished and
for the 1994 assessment year ( the year at issue in this appeal),
the personal property assessment rolls indicate a value to the
personal property of $55, 343.
Nancy Vincent, GDR' s representative, introduced a detailed
appraisal which set forth its consideration of the appraisal
procedures. The appraisal included material relating to the market
data approach, the income approach, and the cost approach to value.
A copy of the appraisal report was provided to the Assessor along
with any subsequent corrections or written explanations thereto.
The appraisal provided by GDR includes the actual 1993
operating income, the actual rent roll as of January 1994, and the
actual operating expenses for 1990 through 1993.
In the income approach to value, the appraiser used the
reported 1993 income of $ 311, 196. He deducted expenses of
206, 355 to show a net operating income of $ 104, 841. This he
capitalized at a 10 percent rate to determine a property value of
1, 048, 410. In support, the appraiser included the printed rent
roll for the 73 units which shows a monthly gross income of
28, 593.
As additional support, the appraiser provided printed material
which was published by the Cain & Scott Appraisal Reporting
Service.
Using the Cain & Scott data, the appraiser determined a
property value of $1, 260, 875 for the subject. Again, a 10 percent
capitalization rate was used.
In support of market data, the Appraiser introduced three
sales of apartment complexes which in summary are:

Assessor offered into evidence three sales of improved properties.
All data relating to these three sales has been provided for this
Board' s review. A summary of the three sales is as follows:
Sale NO. 1, Edgewood Villa Apartments, located one mile east
of the subject, Bold December 1991, for $1, 900, 000. The total
building size is 61, 714 square feet consisting of 88 units. This
sale reflects $30. 79 per square foot or $21, 591 per unit before
consideration of adjustments. After adjusting for factors
considered inferior to the subject, the indicated value determined
by the Assessor is $36. 95 per square foot or $25, 909 per unit.
Sale No. 2, known as the Manchester Heights Apartments, is
located five miles south of the subject and was consummated in July
1990, for $1, 070, 000. There is a total of 28, 652 square feet in
this complex made up of 34 units. The indicated per square foot
value is $ 37. 34 and the per unit price is $ 34, 516, before
adjustments. The Assessor concluded that this sale was very
comparable to the subject and no adjustments were made.
Sale No. 3 is of the Olympic Glenn Apartments located five
miles south of the subject. This sale was consummated February
1993, for $1, 589, 561. There is a total of 61, 122 square feet in
this complex thus indicating a price per square foot of $26. This
complex has 78 units for a unit value of $ 20, 379. The Assessor
made no adjustments to this sale.
It is the Assessor' s opinion, from the analysis of these
sales, that the value indicated to the subject property is $35 per
square foot or $23, 000 per unit.
In the income approach to value the Assessor utilized her
opinion of market data. She estimated the potential gross income
of $ 390, 696 less vacancy of $46, 884 to arrive an effective gross
income of $343, 812. From this she deducted estimated expenses of
154, 715 to arrive at a net income of $ 189, 097 which she
capitalized at a 10 percent capitalization rate indicating a value
to the total property of $1, 842, 000.
In the reconstructed cost approach to value, the Assessor
determined a value to the property of $1, 745, 000.

This Board' B goal in its hearings is the acquisition of
sufficient, accurate evidence to support a determination of true
and fair value as defined by statute ( RCW 84. 40. 030) and the
Washington Administrative Code ( WAC 458- 12- 301) .
When available, comparable sales are the preferred evidence of
value. Comparable sales closest to the lien date are given the
most weight.
Market value is best derived from the analysis of sales of
similar properties. Income and cost approaches will only be given
substantial weight in the absence of adequate market data.
liThe sales comparison approach is based on the premise that
the market value of a property is directly related to the prices of
comparable, competitive properties. The value of a property in the
market is set by the availability of substitute properties of
similar utility and desirability. II Appraisal Institute, The
DDraisal of Re~l Rs~arp 403 ( lOth ed. 1992)
This Board, in reviewing all of the evidence presented by
each party, concludes that the income approach to value offers the
best evidence. We note that in the income approach to value each
party has started with the same gross income. The differences lie
in what is judged tv be reasonable vacancy rates, expenses, and
other factors of cost of doing business. We follow the guide of
the Assessor' s market income approach to value, however,
recognizing a higher expense ratio than considered by the Assessor
and as supported by the report of actual expenses.

DECISJ;QIi
In Docket No. 48326, the decision of the Board of Equalization
is affirmed. In Docket NO. 48327, the Board of Equalization' s
decision is set aside. In this Board' s analysis, the total

886, 000 to the improvement.
The Kitsap County Assessor and Treasurer are hereby directed
that the assessment and tax rolls of Kitsap County are to accord
with and give full effect to the provisions of this decision.
